1. Welcome: See What You Will Build

odeComponent.htmlView:
Welcome: See What You Will Build

Welcome to Basics in Webpage Making. This module is designed for beginners who are comfortable using a computer but have little or no experience creating webpages. Instead of treating HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as three disconnected subjects, you will use them to build one small webpage from beginning to end. Each section adds a new layer to the same project so you can see exactly what each technology contributes.

The finished page below is your destination. HTML will provide the heading, navigation, sections, links, image, button, and text. CSS will improve the colors, spacing, typography, and layout. JavaScript will make the practice button respond to a click. You do not need to install programming software or use a command line. When an activity includes the embedded editor, you can change the starter code and view the result directly in your browser.

Work through the screens in order the first time. Read the explanation, inspect the example, and then complete the short activity. When you experiment with code, change one thing at a time and look at the output before making another change. This makes it easier to understand cause and effect and easier to recover when a typo causes unexpected behavior.

Key ideas

  • One continuous webpage grows throughout the module.
  • Practice happens directly in the browser.
  • Knowledge checks provide immediate feedback.
  • The final activity combines structure, style, and interaction.

Your task

Preview the completed webpage. Notice its structure, visual styling, and the button that changes the message. You will build these layers step by step.

Quick check: What is the main project you will complete?

One small working webpage that combines HTML structure, CSS styling, and a JavaScript interaction.

Basics in Webpage Making · Screen 1 of 20

Objectives, the Three-Language Connection, and Pre-Check

A browser combines HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into one experience, but each language has a different responsibility. HTML describes what is on the page and how the content is organized. CSS describes how that content should look and how it should be arranged. JavaScript adds behavior, such as changing text after a visitor selects a button. Keeping these roles clear will help you decide where a change belongs when you build or debug a page.

By the end of the module, you should be able to identify the purpose of all three technologies, create the basic structure of a webpage with HTML, apply CSS to change appearance and layout, add one simple JavaScript interaction, and explain how the three pieces work together. The goal is a practical foundation, not memorization of every tag, property, or programming feature.

The short pre-check below is not graded. It simply helps you notice what you already know. If a question feels unfamiliar, that is expected; each answer will be covered later. After the pre-check, you will meet the embedded code editor and begin with the structural layer: HTML.

Key ideas

  • HTML = structure and meaning.
  • CSS = presentation and layout.
  • JavaScript = behavior and interaction.
  • The browser combines all three into the page the learner sees.

Your task

Ask whether the change concerns structure/content, visual presentation, or behavior.

Basics in Webpage Making · Screen 2 of 20

Meet the Embedded Code Editor

The embedded editor lets you practice without installing software. It has three code areas—HTML, CSS, and JavaScript—and an output preview. During the HTML section, your attention will stay mostly on the HTML pane, as CSS and JavaScript will not play a role until their designated section.

The preview updates after you type, and the Run button lets you refresh it immediately. Reset restores the starter code for the current activity. Reset is useful when several changes make the example difficult to repair. An error does not mean you failed; it is information. Compare the code with the example, check punctuation and closing tags, and try again.

This module uses the same small webpage repeatedly. That means code from one stage will appear again later with new additions. You are not expected to preserve your edits from one screen to the next. Each activity starts with the version needed for that lesson, allowing you to focus on the new concept without rebuilding everything.

Code editors are a good way to get started when it comes to making webpages. It allows you to see and change elements as needed. Please check

Key ideas

  • Edit code in the labeled pane.
  • Use Run to refresh the output immediately.
  • Use Reset to return to the activity's starter code.
  • Read error messages and inspect the smallest recent change first.

Your task

Change “My Web Learning Page” to a title of your choice, then change the paragraph. Confirm that the preview changes while the CSS and JavaScript panes remain untouched.

Quick check: What should you use if you want the original activity code back?

Use Reset. It restores the starter code for that activity.

odeComponent.htmlView:
The Basics of HTML

First let's start off with what HTML is. HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. This may seem like random words, but it does have meaning behind it. HyperText, the 'HT', simply refers to text that has links, references, and other extra aspects that regular text may not have. Markup Language, the 'ML', is a shorthand way of saying that the language itself can change and give structure to the HyperText. 

HTML is mostly composed of tags. Tags is what gives structure and order to the document, and allows you to give special meaning to each element. Tags are defined like the following: "<tag> </tag>". Before we get into structure, let us go over basic tags and what they do.

Tags typically have an opening and closing of them. An opening is simply the name encapsulated with a less than and greater than symbol like so: "<tag>". Tags are then closed in a similar fashion, but with a slash before the tag's name, like so: "</tag>". This is useful as you can put content in between the start and closing tag.

Key ideas

  • Understand what HTML stands for.
  • Understand what HTML means.
  • Understand what a tag is in HTML and how it is formatted.

Your task

Complete the fill-in-the-blanks activity below from what you've learnt in the block of code above. Then, continue with this section.

HTML is an acronym meaning different things. The H stands for the word @@Hyper@@, and the T stands for the word @@Text@@. The M is for @@Markup@@, and finally, the L stands for @@Language@@.

An example of a tag in this language would "<tagname>":, with a matching closing tag being <@@/tagname@@>. A closing tag always has a @@slash@@ before the name.

The Basic Tags of HTML

Here are some basic tags and what they do:

<p> - Stands for "paragraph," allows you to put simple, regular text. Example: "<p>This is paragraph text!</p>"

<h1> - Stands for "header," with the 1 signifying it's the largest type of header. Numbers range from 1-6, with a smaller number leading to a smaller header. Example: "<h2>This Is a Header!</h2>"

<title> - Stands for "title," titles your webpage, and is typically found at the head / top of your document. Example: "<title>This is a title</title>"

<head>, <body> - Separate, but main sections of your document, with different parts going into each. More information on the next sub module.

<div> - Stands for "division", allows for grouping and advanced structure.

<html> - Main section, all other tags should be placed within this one, everything within is defined as part of the document, though, more will be discussed during the next section.

Key ideas

  • Understand how the given tag structure applies to HTML.
  • Remember some of the basic tags in HTML.
  • Know how to use said basic tags of HTML.

The Basic HTML Document Structure

A complete HTML page follows a specific document structure. Before there are any major tags, you must put "<!DOCTYPE html>". This tells the browser to use modern HTML. This is a tag. Last submodule, you learnt all about tags. Unlike the previous tag structure, this is a standalone tag, which don't require a closing tag. Some other standalone tags include:

  • <br> - Placed in paragraphs or other large text clumps in order to start a new line.
  • <hr> - Makes a horizontal line to break sections up.
  • <img> - Allows you to place an image in your document.

Earlier, we discussed the html tag. The <html> tag wraps the whole document. Inside it, the <head> stores information about the page, like <link> tags and the <title>. An snippet of an HTML head should look like this:

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Website</title>
    <link rel="icon" type="png" href="my_favicon.png" />
<head>

The <title> inside the head names the browser tab. The character-set meta element helps the browser interpret text correctly, and the viewport meta element helps the page scale on phones and tablets. The <link> provides a favicon, which is an image / icon next to the title. These lines are not visually exciting, but they are part of a dependable starting template. Notice also that most HTML elements have an opening tag and a closing tag, and nested elements are indented so their relationships are easier to read.

HTML describes meaning before appearance. At this stage, the page may look plain because CSS has not been added. That is okay. Your first goal is a correctly organized document that the browser can understand. Styling comes after the structure is in place. HTML can be seen as the skeleton of the document, meaning that as long as it is there, there is something the browser can recognize.

The <body> element stores what's meant to be visible. For example, paragraphs and headers are put there. They are also found in this nested format. You may take a look below in the provided code editor.

Key ideas

  • Put page information in <head>.
  • Put visible page content in <body>.
  • Nest tags carefully and keep indentation consistent.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Some Extra Information

These activities should give you a grasp on how HTML should be structured. You may practice more using the code editor above or the code editor on the next page.

One more important thing to note is a few things about HTML that have been either seen or will be seen from now on.

  • Elements and tags can have attributes. It typically looks like <tag attribute="setting"> ... </tag>. One example of this is in an <img> tag, you can set a properties like src which is the image's file name and alt that gives a description. Here is an example of this in action: <img scr="Chart.png" alt="A picture of a chart">
  • HTML does have comments. Any text between '<!--' and '-->' will be seen as a comment and not rendered by the Browser.
  • One more important thing is the anchor tag. You can put the anchor tag around something to make it a link to something else. This can be anything, from images, to paragraphs, to divs. An example of this is: <a href="MyOtherPage.html"><p>Click this to go to my other page!</p></a>.
Quick check: Where should a visible paragraph normally be placed?

Inside the <body> element.

HTML Guided Practice and Knowledge Check

You have now seen the major HTML pieces needed for the course project. This screen gives you a chance to apply them together before moving to CSS. Begin by reading the existing structure rather than immediately typing. Identify the head, body, header, main content, sections, links, image, list, and footer. Being able to recognize structure is as important as being able to create it.

For the guided practice, personalize the webpage while preserving its organization. Change the page title and main heading, rewrite one paragraph, add a third resource link, and verify that the image still has meaningful alternative text. If the preview changes unexpectedly, inspect the tag you changed most recently. Look for a missing closing angle bracket, quotation mark, or end tag.

After practicing, complete the knowledge check. The questions focus on the purpose of the HTML elements used in this project. A perfect score is not required to continue, but if you miss a question, use the feedback to return to the relevant example. CSS will depend on the HTML structure you have just built, so this is a good point to confirm the foundation.

Key ideas

  • Recognize the document structure before editing it.
  • Keep visible content inside the body.
  • Use meaningful headings, links, and image alternatives.
  • Debug the most recent small change first.

odeComponent.htmlView:
An Introduction to Styles

From the previous sections, it can be seen on how HTML can set up a page. However, these setups typically lack colors, layout, and styles. That's because styling is the job of CSS, which stands for Cascading Style Sheet. The reason it is called this is because the page is a sheet composed of many style rules that 'cascade' in a way, with broad rules being overtaken by more specific rules.

In this submodule, you will learn some basic CSS rules, properties, and values, and then show how to connect to HTML. More advanced items will come in the following pages / submodules. First though, let's go over how a CSS should look like.

The following is an example of how CSS is written:

* {
    color: green;
}
p {
    color: blue;
    font-family: Arial;
    font-size: 12px;
}
.className {
    border: solid 1px red;
    display: box;
}
#idName {
    color: black;
    font-size: 20px;
}
h1 {
    color: pink !important;
}

That's an example of how CSS interacts with HTML. In the above example, it sets the color of all things like text green, then it makes all paragraph items blue, Arial, and 12px in font size. It then styles all elements with the class 'className' to have red border and be a box. Afterwards, it then styles an element with the id "idName". Finally, it declares something a rule as important.

For now, the rule of thumb is that the important flag is the most specific, and will take the most priority, then ids, then classes, then general items, then finally, with the lowest priority being Universal / General Rules.

Below will be more properties and values, however, they should be obvious based off the name of them alone. In addition, some of them will be things you've seen from the example above.

Key ideas

  • What is CSS for.
  • How CSS works, and what CSS does.
  • How CSS connects to HTML.

Your task

Knowing what you know about CSS so far, complete the activity below and continue to the next text.

One More Style Option

There is one more single style modifier that should be known that has a special importance. That's inline style, where the style is directly in the HTML item like so:
<p style="color:red;"> This is my text! </p>

This is important because of it's priority listing. It falls between the !important tag and an id css ruling in terms of important, meaning it will override anything unless there is a !important tag on something that changes its style.

CSS has a priority list in which certain style rules take priority over the other. For example, it is well know that @@!important Flagged@@ styles have the most importance. On the other end of things, @@Universal@@ styles have the least priority.

The thing with the second most priority is @@Inline@@ styles, which can be found in the HTML document instead of the CSS.

Below that are styles dictated by @@ID@@, then styles dictated by @@Class@@. Finally, that leaves the style with the second lowest priority, which are style tailored for @@General Item@@s.

Further Things to Note

Typically, elements and tags in HTML documents are given either classes or ids in order to style them, with classes being the most prevalent since it works well with JavaScript, which we will get into in its own section.

One thing to note though is if there are two things of the same priority, whatever is lower on the list will be the style that is applied.

  • CSS in relation to the future subject of the course.
  • How styles with the same priority interact.

Add Colors and Fonts

Last section, the basics of CSS was covered. Now, it's time to talk about the colors and fonts that CSS can set. These texts can be paragraphs, headers, or even applied to the parent of a text element that it can then apply to. Here is a list of some basic things you can change for a text that can be set by CSS.

color: Can add color to a text, by either giving any color value.
font-family: Changes the font of a text.
font-size: Changes the size of a font given a value.
font-style: Can give a font a style, like italics.
font-weight: Can bold a font given a value from 100-1000, with a higher value being bolder.
text-decoration: Can add decor like an underline or strikethrough.

That's generally it, but a few extra tips:

  • A color value can be given by things like a hex value ('#FF0000'), an rgb ('rgb(255, 0, 0)'), an hsl ('hsl(0, 100%, 50%)'), or just by name ('red').
  • The font-family property can be given a chain of fonts separated by commas, so if the first one fails to be loaded, it will load the next one in line. Make sure to use web-safe fonts, or fonts that most computers can recognize and has the files for!
  • The font-weight property can also be given a name value as well, like 'bold'.

Key ideas

  • Use font size and line height to support readability.
  • Ensure that your text is proper when styled.

Add Colors and Fonts

Color and typography create visual identity, but their first job is readability. A small, consistent palette usually produces a stronger design than many unrelated colors. In this project, a dark neutral, teal accent, white surface, and light background create clear visual roles.

Contrast matters. Text must be easy to distinguish from its background, and links should remain recognizable. Avoid using color as the only signal for an important state. The example navigation links are white and bold against a dark header, while ordinary links use a teal color against white. Font size and line height also help learners scan longer explanations without crowding the page.

CSS lets you change these choices without altering the document's meaning. The <h1> remains the primary heading whether it is 32 or 52 pixels tall. This is one reason you should choose HTML elements for structure and CSS for appearance. As you edit, compare the result with the original and ask whether your new combination is easier or harder to read.

Key ideas

  • Use a small, purposeful color palette.
  • Maintain strong text/background contrast.
  • Use font size and line height to support readability.
  • Do not choose an HTML element merely for its default appearance.

Your task

Change the main header color, heading size, and body line height. Keep the page readable, then compare your version with Reset.

Quick check: Should you use an <h3> just because you like its default size?

No. Choose heading levels for structure, then control the visual size with CSS.

Basics in Webpage Making · Text 2 of 2 · Screen 8 of 20

Add Spacing and Page Layout

Spacing and layout turn a collection of elements into an organized page. Margin creates space outside an element, while padding creates space inside its border. The box-sizing property can make widths easier to predict. In the project, generous padding keeps text away from card edges, while margins separate one section from another. These choices create visual grouping without adding extra HTML.

Layout also needs to respond to available space. A max-width keeps long text from stretching across an extremely wide monitor, while automatic left and right margins center the content. Images can use width: 100% and height: auto so they scale with their container. A media query can reduce padding on a narrow screen. Responsive design does not require a completely different mobile page; it adapts the same content.

The CSS below also adds rounded corners and a subtle shadow to the content sections. Those details are optional decoration, but the spacing and responsive width directly support usability. Try not to solve layout with repeated
elements or spaces in HTML. Use CSS because spacing is a presentation decision.

Key ideas

  • Margin = outside space; padding = inside space.
  • Use max-width to keep reading lines comfortable.
  • Make images flexible instead of forcing a large fixed width.
  • Use media queries for targeted narrow-screen adjustments.

Your task

More on Page Layout and Spacing

Another thing that can be used is using a flexbox. By applying 'flex' to display, then by applying a 'flex direction,' you can then style it by using things like "justify-content" and "align-items", which can be set to center to automatically center things. Justify content goes by major axis and aligning goes by the minor axis, which is set by the flex direction.

Another way is by setting margin to auto on its sides. When margin is given two values, it applies the first value is applied to the top and bottom, while the second value is applied to the left and right. For example, 'margin: 0px auto;' sets the top and bottom to nothing, but automatically setting the left and right to center it. Do note, that the 'auto' keyword does different things to different items, make sure to search what it does in certain contexts or test it out to see what it does.

Additionally, when you get more advanced, you can use media queries to set special CSS rules for when things get certain sizes.

Key ideas

  • Know how to use margins and padding to your pages benefit.
  • Remember to know how to style your content.

CSS Practice, Before-and-After, and Knowledge Check

This CSS checkpoint asks you to transform the same HTML without rewriting its content. First, use Reset and look at the unstyled version mentally: the information is present, but the hierarchy relies mostly on default browser styles. Then run the provided stylesheet. Color, spacing, width, typography, and card treatment make the same information easier to scan. This before-and-after comparison shows why CSS is a separate layer rather than a replacement for HTML.

For guided practice, make three deliberate changes: choose a new accent color, adjust the section spacing, and change one typography rule. Avoid changing every value. A focused redesign makes it easier to explain what each property did. Check the page at a narrow browser width before you finish so your choices do not create horizontal scrolling or unreadable text.

The knowledge check reviews selectors, the stylesheet connection, spacing, and responsive design. If a CSS rule seems to have no effect, first verify that its selector matches the intended HTML and that the property name and value are valid. Debugging the connection is usually faster than randomly changing several rules.

Key ideas

  • CSS changes presentation without changing the underlying information.
  • Focused changes are easier to test than a complete redesign at once.
  • Responsive behavior should be checked at more than one width.
  • When a rule fails, verify the selector before rewriting the page.

Basics in Webpage Making · Screen 10 of 20

What JavaScript Adds to the Page

While you've learnt HTML and CSS, or the base and style of a page, there is one more piece. Interactability, which belongs to JavaScript. JavaScript is a programming language which can give your website a bit more flare. For example, remember classes from earlier?

JavaScript can change the class of things, and by extension, the style, which applies immediately. Here's an example of that in action!

document.getElementById("elementId").classList.remove("classA");
document.getElementById("elementId").classList.add("classB");

This code does a lot, so allow it to be broken down. First 'document' refers to the document the script is called from. Next, 'getElementById' is a function that given a valid Id, it will pull that element in the code. Finally, the 'classList' part access that element's class list and removes, then adds different classes via their respective functions. It also could have been written as so:

let myElement = document.getElementById("elementId");
myElement.classList.remove("classA");
myElement.classList.add("classB");

This time, it uses the "let" variable to assign that element to a variable called "myElement," then using the variable to access its class list and change it there.

Key ideas

  • JavaScript can change the behaviors of a page.

Here are a few things you should learn about JS:

// comments are started by two slashes...
let x = 20; // let can declare variables like this...
const y = 30; // const can declare constants like so!

console.log(x + y); // And console.log can log things out!

What does this log out? @@50@@

Great! Let's try another example. This is a for loop. Reading the top of it, it counts from 0 to 9, since it starts at 0 and runs for any number below 10, but then counts up by 1 for each run.

let number = 0;
for (let count = 0; count < 10; count++) {
    number = number + count;
}
console.log(number);

What does this log out? @@45@@

Splendid job! One more example should do the trick. This time it works with an if-statement, which only runs if the condition given is true. If not, it runs whatever comes in the 'else' part.

let value = 17;
if (value - 16 < 5) {
    console.log("This number is smaller than 21.");
} else {
    console.log("This number is greater than 20.");
}

What JavaScript Adds to the Page

The webpage already has structure and visual design, but it behaves mostly like a document. JavaScript adds the ability to respond after the page loads. It can react to a click, read information from a form, change text, add or remove a CSS class, or perform calculations. This module uses one small interaction so you can understand the connection without turning the project into a large programming exercise.

JavaScript works with values and instructions. A const declaration can store a reference that will not be reassigned, while let can store a value that needs to change later. You will not need advanced data structures here. The important idea is that JavaScript can locate an HTML element through the browser's Document Object Model, commonly called the DOM, and then read or change that element.

The project will add a practice card containing a paragraph and button. HTML will create those elements, CSS will style them, and JavaScript will change the paragraph after the button is selected. The behavior is intentionally simple because the learning objective is to understand the relationship among the technologies.

Key ideas

  • JavaScript adds behavior after the page loads.
  • The DOM is the browser's representation of the HTML page.
  • JavaScript can select an element and change its content.
  • Keep beginner interactions small enough to explain clearly.

Your task

Read the new practice-card HTML. Identify the paragraph id and button id that JavaScript will use later. Do not worry about writing the event yet.

Quick check: What new capability does JavaScript add to this project?

It allows the page to respond to a user's action and change content.

Understand Simple Events

An event is something that happens in the page, such as a click, key press, input change, or form submission. JavaScript can listen for an event and run a function when it occurs. For the course project, the important event is a button click. The browser waits until the visitor selects the button, then runs the instructions associated with that click.

The addEventListener method is a common way to connect an element to an event. Its first argument names the event, such as "click", and the second argument is the function that should run. The function is sometimes called a callback because the browser calls it later when the event happens. This separates loading the page from responding to user behavior.

In the editor, the button and paragraph already exist in HTML. CSS already controls how the button looks. Your JavaScript will connect behavior to the existing structure. This division is important: HTML does not need an entirely new button just because you want new behavior, and JavaScript does not need to define every color or spacing value.

Key ideas

  • Events represent user or browser actions.
  • addEventListener connects an event to a callback.
  • A click handler runs when the user activates the element.
  • Keep appearance in CSS and behavior in JavaScript when possible.

Your task

Run the example and click the button. Then change only the message inside the callback and run it again. Confirm that the page responds with your new text.

Quick check: When does the callback in a click listener run?

It runs when the selected element receives the click event.

Select Page Elements and Respond to a Button

Before JavaScript can change a page element, it needs a reference to that element. document.getElementById("practiceMessage") asks the DOM for the element whose id is practiceMessage. Saving the result in a clearly named constant gives later code an easy way to use that element. IDs should be unique within the page so the connection is predictable.

Once you have the element reference, textContent can replace its visible text. The first example on this screen changes the paragraph immediately when the script runs. The second step connects that change to the button event. Together, selection and events form a basic interaction pattern: find the elements, listen for the user action, then update the page.

When this pattern fails, check the connection points. Does the HTML contain the exact id that JavaScript requests? Did you spell getElementById correctly? Is the event listener attached to the button rather than the paragraph? Small naming mismatches are common beginner errors and usually easier to find when the variables have descriptive names.

Key ideas

  • Element IDs provide stable hooks for beginner JavaScript.
  • Store selected elements in descriptive variables.
  • textContent changes the text inside an element.
  • Check exact spelling when the script cannot find an element.

Your task

First run the selection-only example, then replace it with the click listener shown in the lesson. Make the button update the paragraph only after it is selected.

Quick check: What does document.getElementById("tipButton") return?

A reference to the HTML element whose id is tipButton, if that element exists.

Review How HTML, CSS, and JavaScript Connect

You have now worked with each technology separately. The next step is to see the project as a connected system. HTML supplies the content and useful hooks, CSS selects that HTML and defines visual rules, and JavaScript selects HTML through the DOM and responds to events. The finished webpage feels unified even though the three layers have different responsibilities.

Consider the practice button. HTML creates the <button> and gives it the id tipButton. CSS selects button elements and controls padding, colors, borders, and hover behavior. JavaScript uses the id to find that same button and attaches a click listener. When the learner clicks, JavaScript updates the paragraph that HTML created. The browser redraws the page using the existing CSS rules.

This separation helps debugging. If the button is missing completely, inspect the HTML. If it exists but looks wrong, inspect the CSS. If it looks correct but does nothing, inspect the JavaScript and the IDs that connect it to the HTML. Starting with the layer responsible for the symptom is more efficient than changing all three at once.

Key ideas

  • HTML answers: what is on the page?
  • CSS answers: how does it look and arrange itself?
  • JavaScript answers: what happens when the user interacts?
  • Debug by matching the symptom to the responsible layer.

Your task

Use the connection map, then explain the button to yourself in three sentences: one for HTML, one for CSS, and one for JavaScript.

Build the Final Webpage: Structure and Content

The final build begins with the HTML foundation. Your goal is not to invent a completely new project; it is to assemble the same pieces you have practiced into a coherent page. The starter structure includes a header, navigation, About section, practice card, resources section, image, and footer. Before touching CSS or JavaScript, read the page from top to bottom and confirm that the content order makes sense without styling.

Make the page your own while preserving its learning requirements. Change the site heading and introductory sentence. Rewrite the About paragraph. Add or replace one resource link. Keep the image's alternative text meaningful, maintain a visible label on the interactive button, and preserve the IDs practiceMessage and tipButton because the JavaScript on the next screen will depend on them.

This is also a good accessibility check. Headings should describe the page hierarchy, link text should be understandable without relying on “click here,” and navigation should use real links. A well-structured page should remain understandable even if every CSS rule is temporarily removed. That is a useful test of whether HTML is carrying the right responsibility.

Key ideas

  • Build a logical reading order before styling.
  • Keep interactive IDs stable when JavaScript depends on them.
  • Use descriptive link text and meaningful image alternatives.
  • Make sure the page still makes sense without CSS.

Your task

Personalize the final HTML structure and content. Do not change the CSS or JavaScript yet. Run the page and verify the complete content flow.

Quick check: Why should the final page make sense even without CSS?

Because HTML should provide meaningful structure and content independently of presentation.

Build the Final Webpage: Styling and Interaction

Now add the final two layers to the HTML you just reviewed. The stylesheet provides the visual system: a responsive header, readable content width, cards, spacing, image behavior, and button styling. JavaScript provides the interaction: selecting the practice button updates the message and changes the button label. Each layer improves the experience without replacing the work of the others.

Use the editor to make at least one intentional change in each pane. In HTML, personalize one sentence. In CSS, change the accent color or spacing. In JavaScript, rewrite the practice-tip message. Then test the button and shrink the browser width. Your finished page should still be readable, the button should still be easy to identify, and the interaction should produce visible feedback.

Avoid adding complexity only to make the page seem more advanced. The proposal calls for a basic webpage and one simple interactive feature. A polished beginner project with clear code, consistent design, and dependable behavior better demonstrates the learning objectives than a large feature that is difficult to explain or test.

Key ideas

  • Make one controlled change in each language.
  • Test both appearance and behavior.
  • Check the layout at a narrow width.
  • Prefer a clear, dependable interaction over unnecessary complexity.

Your task

Complete the three-layer final build: personalize HTML, adjust one CSS design choice, and rewrite the JavaScript feedback message.

Quick check: What makes this a combined webpage rather than three separate exercises?

The CSS and JavaScript both operate on the same HTML structure to produce one final user experience.

Find and Fix Common Beginner Errors

Small errors are normal in webpage development. HTML problems often come from missing closing tags, misplaced quotation marks, or content placed outside the intended container. CSS problems often come from a selector that does not match the HTML, a misspelled property, or a missing punctuation mark. JavaScript problems often come from an incorrect element ID, a missing parenthesis or brace, or code that runs against an element it cannot find.

A useful debugging strategy is to identify the symptom, choose the most likely layer, and reduce the problem. If the whole section disappears, start with HTML. If the section exists but a color does not apply, start with CSS. If the button appears but does not respond, start with JavaScript. Compare exact names and test after every repair instead of making several guesses at once.

The editor below intentionally contains beginner mistakes. The page heading tag is incomplete, the CSS selector uses the wrong class name, and JavaScript requests an ID that does not exist. Repair one error at a time and run after each fix. The goal is not speed; it is developing a repeatable troubleshooting process you can use on your own page.

Key ideas

  • Read the symptom before editing.
  • Check the responsible layer first.
  • Compare IDs and selectors exactly.
  • Fix one problem, run, and then move to the next.

Your task

Repair the broken heading, make the CSS style the intended card, and make the button update the message.

Quick check: What is the safest way to debug several problems?

Fix and test one small problem at a time, beginning with the layer that matches the symptom.

Final Review and Assessment

The final assessment checks whether you can recognize the roles and connections you used throughout the project. It focuses on the core learning objectives rather than obscure syntax. You should be able to identify HTML structure, connect CSS presentation to that structure, explain a simple event-driven JavaScript interaction, and choose a reasonable first troubleshooting step when the result is not what you expected.

Complete all questions before checking your score. Read the feedback for any item you miss and return to the corresponding section if needed. A useful review strategy is to explain the project without looking at the code: HTML created the page and interaction targets; CSS established a readable, responsive visual design; JavaScript found the button and message, listened for a click, and changed the page.

After the assessment, the final screen shows the completed webpage again and provides resources for continuing. Your next learning goal should be small and specific. For example, rebuild this page from a blank file, add one new section, or create a simple form. The strongest sign that you understand the basics is being able to make a small change and explain which layer should contain it.

Key ideas

  • Focus on responsibilities and connections.
  • Use feedback to revisit a specific weak area.
  • Explain the project in your own words.
  • Choose a small next challenge rather than jumping immediately to a large application.

Your task

Complete the eight-question final assessment. If you miss more than two items, revisit the related practice screens and retake it.

Quick check: What is the core mental model for the whole module?

HTML provides structure, CSS provides presentation, and JavaScript provides behavior.

Completed Webpage, Resources, and Next Steps

You have completed the guided path from a plain HTML document to a styled, interactive webpage. The final version below contains the same features introduced throughout the module: meaningful page structure, headings and paragraphs, navigation and resource links, an image with alternative text, responsive CSS, a clear visual hierarchy, and a JavaScript button response. The important achievement is understanding how those pieces connect, not simply reaching a particular visual design.

Continue by rebuilding the project without copying the starter code. Then make one controlled extension. You might add another section, create a second button with a different response, add a simple form field, or redesign the page while keeping the HTML semantics intact. When you encounter unfamiliar syntax, use a reference rather than trying to memorize the entire language. MDN Web Docs, W3Schools, freeCodeCamp, and Eloquent JavaScript are useful starting points for further practice.

To publish this course project, export the eXeLearning project as a website, test the navigation and interactive editors in more than one browser, and upload the exported site to the hosting location your team selected. Before submission, proofread the pages, verify external links, test the final button and assessments, and confirm that the public URL remains accessible through the required date.

Key ideas

  • Rebuild the page from memory as your first follow-up challenge.
  • Add one new feature at a time.
  • Use reputable references when you need unfamiliar syntax.
  • Test the exported course and public link before submission.

Your task

Interact with the completed page one final time. Then choose one next-step feature you could add and identify whether it belongs in HTML, CSS, or JavaScript.
